title: Arguments at home
hookLine: Jacob walks back toward the brother he cheated: the cooling breath, then the repair face to face
tomorrow: one sister served, one sat and listened. which one got it right?

lines: THY FACE, AS THE FACE OF GOD.
cards: Years after he tricked his brother out of their father's blessing, Jacob is walking toward him, and Esau is coming with four hundred men. Jacob has sent gifts ahead.
Now he goes in front of his family and bows to the ground seven times as he comes near his brother. Then Esau runs to meet him, embraces him, falls on his neck and kisses him, and they weep.
And Jacob says the strangest thing to the brother he wronged: "I have seen thy face, as though I had seen the face of God." Why say that to Esau?

teach.h: I HAVE SEEN GOD FACE TO FACE.
teach.b: Because of the night before. Alone by the ford of the Jabbok, Jacob wrestled with a man until daybreak, and named the place Peniel: "for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved."
One night, in Jacob's words, he sees God face to face. The next morning he sees his brother's face.
The two faces rhyme. Jewish law turns that kind of meeting into a rule.

teach.h: YOM KIPPUR CAN'T SKIP THE PERSON.
teach.b: The Mishnah says Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, atones for wrongs between a person and God, but for wrongs between a person and another person, the day doesn't atone until you make it right with them.
Prayer can't go around the person.

teach.h: TESHUVAH: GO TO THE ONE YOU HURT.
teach.b: That's teshuvah, return, with a home address: you go to the one you hurt. Jacob had sent messengers and gifts ahead, but he doesn't stop there. He walks, bows, and asks Esau to accept his gift.

So that's why Esau's face feels like God's: repair goes through the other person's face, not around it. At home, after a fight, the cooling breath matters. Then comes the walk back toward the face you argued with.

how: Before Yom Kippur, Jews are taught to go to the people they have wronged and ask forgiveness, because Jewish teaching holds that wrongs between people are mended with the person, not only in prayer.

o: waiting until both sides forget about the fight
replacing what got broken with a brand-new one
going back to the person to mend what broke

games.q: Jacob's way back: tap the pairs.
p: ran to meet his brother and kissed him
where Jacob saw God face to face
atones between a person and God
return: go to the one you hurt

s: in Jewish teaching, a sincere prayer settles a wrong against another person
the Mishnah says Yom Kippur doesn't atone for those until you make it right with the person.
Jacob sent gifts ahead before he met Esau
and when they met, he asked Esau to accept them.
Esau made Jacob beg before he forgave him
Jacob bowed, but Esau ran to meet him, embraced him and wept.

games.q: you and your sister fought over your parents' anniversary plans. you've both cooled off. what does Jacob's story say comes next?
o: go to her, face to face, and make it right; repair goes through the person.
let it fade; once you've both cooled off, the fight is effectively over.
write down what you learned; repair is mostly inner work.
games.why: Jacob walked toward the brother he wronged, bowed, and said seeing his face was like seeing the face of God.

practice: Bring to mind one argument at home that hasn't been mended, big or small. Write by hand, or just in your head, the first sentence you'd say walking toward that person, with no but in it.
Then sit with their face in mind until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Arguments at home: the cooling breath first, then the walk back toward the face you argued with. Jacob's way back to Esau.

orig.note: Hebrew: return, repentance; the turning back that Jewish teaching ties to mending wrongs.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: repair, not around the person but through them, face to face. See you tomorrow.
